1. Open the starwars dataset (located in tidyverse)
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
data("starwars")
```

2. Create a scatter plot of character's height and mass. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass))+geom_point(na.rm=TRUE)
```

2a. Change the color and shape of the points in your scatter plot. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass))+geom_point(shape=5, color="purple", na.rm=TRUE)
```

3. Add Homeworld as a third variable to your scatterplot. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color=homeworld))+geom_point(na.rm=TRUE)
```

3a. What do you notice about the graph? (e.g. describe what you see)
Adding a third variable for homeworld makes the graph suddenly gain a large legend for every possible homeworld. The colors make it easy to read, but having the legend be so big can be very overwhelming.

4. Make a boxplot of height. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height))+geom_boxplot(na.rm=TRUE)
```

5. Make a boxplot of height for each species present in the data. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, species))+geom_boxplot(na.rm=TRUE)
```

5a. change the appearance of your graph in at least 3 ways. 
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, color=species))+geom_boxplot(na.rm=TRUE)+labs(x="Height(cms)", y="Species", title="Average Height for Each Species in Starwars")+theme_classic()
```

6. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from viridis.
```{r}
library(viridis)
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color=eye_color))+geom_point(na.rm=TRUE)+scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE, option = "magma")
```

7.Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph that uses a color palette from RColorBrewer.
```{r}
library(RColorBrewer)
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, mass, color=sex)) + geom_point( na.rm = TRUE) + scale_color_brewer(palette="Purples")
```

8. Using any variables in the starwars dataset, create a graph using facet_wrap
```{r}
ggplot(starwars, aes(height, color=sex))+geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE)+facet_wrap(~sex)
```
